articles.title: In 2017, ‘Air Jaws’ photographer Chris Fallows bought South African farmland with his wildlife-art earnings; by 2021, further purchases and land agreements had created a 3,200-acre private nature reserve
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Wildlife photographer Chris Fallows uses his earnings to buy and restore farmland in South Africa, creating a 3,200-acre nature reserve promoting biodiversity and conservation efforts in the region.
articles.body: Wildlife photographers spend careers chasing a few shots that define them, and then, more often than not, they move on to the next assignment. Chris Fallows took a different path. He spent more than two decades photographing one of his best known images, a great white shark hurling itself out of the ocean off the coast of South Africa, before he and his wife, Monique, used the proceeds from that career to buy worn-out farmland and return it to nature.Fallows made his name in 2001 with the image known as Air Jaws, a great white shark breaching captured off Seal Island near Cape Town, a photograph credited with helping inspire the long-running Air Jaws series on the Discovery Channel. His career as a wildlife photographer is profiled by Canon South Africa, for whom he serves as a professional ambassador. Fallows built much of that career around the sharks of False Bay until the population that made his reputation began to vanish from the area about a decade ago, a decline researchers have linked to several causes, including years of heavy fishing pressure on the smaller sharks and other prey that great whites depend on. Researchers have also suggested that at least part of the disappearance may be linked to a small number of orcas that hunt great whites along the same stretch of coast, leaving Fallows without the subject that had defined his working life and searching for a new way to put his photography to use.From ocean conservation to buying up farmlandFallows and his wife could not safeguard the sharks that had disappeared from the waters he knew best, so they decided to apply the same instinct to dry land, arguing that while nobody can control the sea, land can be acquired, fenced and actively managed for the benefit of the creatures living on it. In 2017 the couple used money earned from sales of Chris’s fine art prints to buy a modest plot on the western bank of the Breede River at Cape Infanta, on South Africa’s southern coast, an area badly overrun by introduced acacia and other alien trees planted decades earlier for timber and erosion control. Conservation specialists were brought in to remove the invasive growth, and at first they doubted the native fynbos beneath would recover. Fynbos occurs almost nowhere else on earth and forms the backbone of the Cape Floral Kingdom, one of the richest concentrations of plant diversity on the planet, despite covering only a small strip of South Africa's southern coastline. The outcome of the experiment mattered well beyond the boundaries of one farm.A single farm grows into a much larger reserveWithin a few seasons, the bare alien-choked ground had started to recover into blossoming fynbos, and several neighbouring landowners, some with substantial cattle and crop farms of their own, approached the Fallows about contributing their holdings to the restoration project. Those voluntary agreements, combined with further land purchases, grew the couple's original plot into a private reserve of roughly 3,200 acres by 2021, an area they continue to expand as more landowners sign up, restoring habitat for birds, small mammals and the region's threatened fynbos plant communities in the process. That kind of voluntary, landowner-led expansion mirrors a formal stewardship option available to private landowners across the Western Cape through partnerships coordinated by Cape Nature, the provincial conservation authority, which has helped bring hundreds of thousands of hectares of privately owned land under some form of biodiversity protection over the past two decades.Part of a much bigger vision for connected wildernessThe Fallows never intended the Cape Infanta reserve to be their destination. The couple have since begun purchasing a much larger area of desert country in neighbouring Namibia, using the same model of buying degraded farmland and letting it recover. Their goal is to connect their land to existing conservation areas and cross-border wildlife corridors in southern Africa. That ambition of stitching together isolated private reserves into one continuous landscape echoes the mission pursued for decades by the Peace Parks Foundation, which has been working since the late 1990s to link protected areas across national borders so elephants, big cats and other wide-ranging species can once again roam freely. From a single damaged farm bought with photography money, the project has become a working demonstration of how private conservation land can expand well beyond its original boundaries, one willing neighbour at a time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DEHI: A 21-year-old woman allegedly jumped into the Chenab River in Doda district on Saturday after speaking to her father over the phone and telling him, "This is my life," before saying, "Bye-bye, papa." A joint rescue operation was launched soon after the incident, but there was no immediate trace of her.The incident took place around 2 pm at the Shiva Dal bridge near Prem Nagar. Police, personnel from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and local volunteers joined the search operation in the river after the woman, identified as Payal Devi, reportedly jumped from the bridge.A video purportedly recorded by passersby who attempted to discourage her from taking the step shows Devi saying "bye-bye" before jumping into the Chenab. The video subsequently went viral on social media.Officials said the circumstances that led to Devi taking the extreme step were not immediately known.‘This is my own life’The final conversation between Devi and her father, Krishan Lal, came shortly before she disappeared into the river.According to Lal, Devi had gone to a mela earlier in the day. She later called him and said that she was feeling unwell and intended to consult a doctor.When the doctor was reportedly unavailable, Devi began making her way back. At some point, she apparently got onto a motorcycle.Lal said he subsequently received a call from a person who was accompanying his daughter. The person told him that Devi had run towards the river.The development prompted Lal to speak to his daughter over the phone. He said he repeatedly asked her what had happened and whether somebody had said or done anything to her.Lal recalled Devi telling him, "Nobody should come near me."He continued trying to understand what had happened and urged her to explain why she was behaving that way.According to Lal, Devi responded, "No, papa. This is my own life. My heart tells me that I should go this way."She then told her father, "Bye-bye, papa," before the call ended, he said.Passersby tried to stop herThe moments before Devi jumped were also reportedly captured on video.The video, which was said to have been recorded by passersby at the bridge, shows people attempting to discourage her. Despite their efforts, she reportedly jumped into the Chenab.The footage later circulated widely on social media, drawing attention to the incident and the efforts of those present to prevent her from taking the step.Search operation launchedFollowing the incident, police, SDRF personnel and local volunteers launched a joint rescue operation in the Chenab River.Teams searched the river for Devi, but officials said there was no trace of her.The search operation was undertaken after the reported jump from the Shiva Dal bridge, a location near Prem Nagar in Doda district.As the rescue teams continued their efforts, the reasons behind Devi's actions remained unclear. Officials said the circumstances that led to her decision were not immediately known.Her father's account indicates that she had earlier complained of feeling unwell and had intended to see a doctor, but what happened between that conversation and her reported arrival at the bridge remains unclear.The investigation and search operation are continuing, while authorities are attempting to establish the sequence of events leading up to the incident.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A 14-year-old collected discarded school supplies; 2 years later her nonprofit has 200 branches across 52 countries and 1,000 teen volunteers
articles.summary: US News: When Grace Millard was 14, discarded pencils, half-used notebooks and unwanted art supplies were an everyday sight in the halls of her Connecticut hig.
articles.body: When Grace Millard was 14, discarded pencils, half-used notebooks and unwanted art supplies were an everyday sight in the halls of her Connecticut high school. What caught her attention was not simply the waste, but the contrast surrounding it. Schools and community centres in nearby communities were looking for basic supplies that families could not always afford, while perfectly usable materials were being thrown away. That realisation led Millard and her classmate Jordan Chen to create Restoring Rainbows in 2023, a youth-led nonprofit built around collecting, restoring and redistributing school supplies. Just two years later, Millard, now 16, is co-CEO of an organisation with more than 200 branches across 52 countries and around 1,000 teen volunteers. The initiative has already kept tens of thousands of supplies from landfills while getting them into the hands of children who need them.How discarded school supplies inspired a 14-year-oldMillard's idea began with a simple observation inside her own school. As a 14-year-old freshman, she noticed pencils, notebooks and art materials being abandoned in classrooms and cafeterias, even though other schools and community centres were seeking donations of similar supplies. The contradiction became the starting point for a project that connected sustainability with educational access. Millard and Chen shared an interest in art, climate change and sustainability, and began researching what it would take to establish a nonprofit. They launched Restoring Rainbows in 2023, initially keeping the operation close to home. Their first step was practical, asking local institutions whether they could host collection boxes. According to Points of Light, the pair sent around 30 cold emails to museums, schools, libraries and art galleries before their project began gaining momentum.How Restoring Rainbows gives school supplies a second lifeThe organisation does more than collect unwanted materials. Donated pencils, books, notebooks and art supplies are cleaned, repaired and prepared before being redistributed to schools, after-school programmes and community centres. Millard and Chen initially handled much of the restoration themselves, developing a process that could turn materials destined for rubbish bins into usable resources once again. Books have become one of Millard's favourite items to restore because they often carry traces of their previous owners, from familiar characters to handwritten notes and doodles. Before redistribution, personal information is removed to protect privacy. The model creates a direct link between reducing waste and supporting children who may lack access to school or creative materials. For Millard, the goal is therefore not simply to save supplies from landfills, but to make sure those resources continue to have value in another child's hands.How a 14-year-old turned a school project into 200 branchesThe transformation from a small Connecticut initiative into an international nonprofit accelerated after Millard and Chen began sharing their work online. About six months after starting, they began posting about Restoring Rainbows on social media, where teenagers from different parts of the world started asking how they could participate. Instead of asking everyone to operate directly from Connecticut, the founders developed a branch programme that allowed young people to recreate the model in their own communities. Digital guides, workbooks and video tutorials gave volunteers a framework for collecting and restoring supplies locally. Two years after its creation, Restoring Rainbows had grown to more than 200 branches spanning 52 countries, supported by about 1,000 teen volunteers. The network has kept tens of thousands of restored supplies out of landfills and distributed them to children and communities that need them.Why discarded school supplies became a global youth movementMillard's experience has turned discarded school supplies into a wider lesson about sustainability, creativity and youth-led action. Restoring Rainbows now has volunteers sharing its work from countries including El Salvador and India, showing how a local waste problem can become a global community effort. Millard believes education about sustainability matters alongside the number of supplies donated, and the organisation is working towards distributing 100,000 school supplies. Its wider mission also reflects her belief that art can connect children across differences in language and culture while encouraging confidence, empathy and creativity. Despite running the nonprofit alongside high school, Millard plans to remain involved through college and beyond, with structures in place for younger leaders to eventually continue the mission. Her message is straightforward, young people do not have to wait until they are older or feel completely prepared before acting on an idea that matters to them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, smoke grounded civilian aircraft as 242 people were trapped by California’s Creek Fire; National Guard crews rescued all 242 in 7 hours, the largest helicopter rescue in Guard history
articles.summary: US News: It’s been six years since the Creek Fire rescue changed nighttime firefighting forever, after California National Guard crews flew into a wall of fire.
articles.body: It’s been six years since the Creek Fire rescue changed nighttime firefighting forever, after California National Guard crews flew into a wall of fire and smoke in the largest helicopter rescue in Guard history and saved all of them in seven hours. A new mini-documentary shared by Governor Gavin’s office recounts the extraordinary nighttime mission that rescued 242 people.The extraordinary nighttime rescueIt started on September 4, 2020, in the Sierra National Forest and burned with the kind of speed that leaves no time for evacuation protocols. By Labor Day weekend, hundreds of people were fleeing for their lives as flames surrounded Mammoth Pool Reservoir. The smoke was so thick that civilian pilots couldn’t risk flying. As evening fell, the options began to narrow. The people were still there, and the fire showed no signs of calming down. Hundreds of people were stranded. Leaving fate to decide the lives of 242 people wasn’t an option the California National Guard (CalGuard) aircrews were considering. So the CalGuard crew from the 40th Combat Aviation Brigade decided to fly into the fire after dark. Their only edge? Night-vision goggles.CH-47 Chinook and UH-60 Black Hawk crews suited up and prepared for what no one had seriously attempted before: flying combat helicopters into an active wildfire zone at night. Flying into the wildfire alone was risk enough; the fire and smoke only worsened it. They relied on infrared goggles and radio communication.The risk was real. The pilots had to land on a steep boat ramp with flames closing in. People waiting for rescue had severe burns. Some were so badly burned that they were unable to walk. The smoke was impossible. Even with the night-vision goggles, the crews were essentially flying into a wall. But they flew anyway.Over the next seven hours, the pilots made multiple runs through smoke-filled airspace. They got people aboard, got everyone strapped down and pulled up before the fire got any closer. There was no scope for second chances or do-overs. With no room for errors, the crew stuck to its discipline and training, and moved fast enough and steadily enough to pull it off in the dark. The mission saved 242 lives.A mini-documentary, ‘Beyond the Limits: Creek Fire Rescue’, was released, which tells the story of the rescue through the eyes of the pilots and flight crews who carried out the mission. It shows how they made life-or-death decisions as the fire closed in.How the rescue opened new possibilities in nighttime wildfire responseThe rescue undoubtedly became historic in California’s evolution of nighttime wildfire response. The rescue showed what was possible when specialised military aviation capabilities could operate after dark. Today, California continues to expand nighttime aviation capabilities, training CAL FIRE and Cal Guard crews who work together around the clock when wildfires threaten communities.“I am proud of the dedicated service members of the California National Guard, who humbly serve alongside our interagency partners in the fight against wildfires. Together, through coordination and shared purpose, we support those leading the response to protect our communities,” CalGuard Major General Matthew Beevers said in a statement.The rescue team was recognised with the Distinguished Flying Cross and the California Medal of Valor for their extraordinary service.The rescue was a collective effort. The Cal Guard aircrews worked alongside CAL FIRE, the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES), local fire departments, law enforcement, emergency medical providers and other partners on the ground to coordinate intelligence, evacuations, medical care and logistics. Teams on the ground provided critical intelligence, evacuation support, medical care and logistics as the Guard crews worked from the air."The Creek Fire rescue showed us what's possible when agencies unite in the face of crisis. The collaboration between CAL FIRE, the California National Guard, Cal OES, local responders, and countless partners was more than a coordinated effort—it was a testament to the power of partnership. Our ongoing commitment to training, innovation, and teamwork ensures that when Californians need us most, we stand ready—stronger together," CAL FIRE Chief Deputy Director of Operations Anale Burlew said."California's first responders and emergency managers answer the call to serve their communities every day, often stepping forward during the most difficult and dangerous moments. Cal OES is proud to have supported the heroic actions of the California National Guard aircrews during the Creek Fire by coordinating across agencies and disciplines, so they had the support they needed to protect lives, safeguard communities, and keep Californians safe when it mattered most," Cal OES Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs added.And needless to say, the Creek Fire became a defining moment in how California approaches nighttime wildfire aviation.Since the Creek Fire in 2020, California has expanded its wildfire response capabilities. CAL FIRE now operates aircraft with nighttime capability, including a fleet of 17 S-70i Fire Hawk helicopters, eight exclusive-use contracted air tankers and two additional night-flying coordination helicopters. CAL FIRE and the California National Guard regularly train together so that military aviation can be safely integrated into wildfire operations when additional resources are needed.California has also expanded the use of advanced fire intelligence, mapping and detection tools, including ALERTCalifornia, FIRIS and the Cal Guard’s FireGuard programme, which support statewide wildfire detection, assessment and intelligence.Now they have a more connected system, with firefighters, pilots, emergency managers, military crews and technology teams working together when impossible conditions show up. And it all started with the rescue mission in 2020!Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Billionaire Mitchell Rales gave $116 million to the National Gallery of Art; the record gift will send artworks to museums across America
articles.summary: US News: A $116 million gift from billionaire and National Gallery of Art trustee Mitchell P. Rales is set to transform how people across the United States exp.
articles.body: A $116 million gift from billionaire and National Gallery of Art trustee Mitchell P. Rales is set to transform how people across the United States experience some of the country's most important artworks. The Mitchell P. Rales Family Foundation has given the National Gallery of Art a transformational gift to permanently endow Across the Nation, the museum's nationwide lending programme. Launched in 2025, the initiative allows regional museums to select works from the National Gallery's permanent collection for long-term loans, bringing masterpieces to communities far beyond Washington, DC. The National Gallery of Art announced the historic gift on April 21, 2026, describing it as the largest gift to endow programming in the institution's history, comparable in scale with its original founding gifts. Made during America's 250th anniversary year, the endowment will allow the programme to continue in perpetuity and eventually bring works from the National Gallery's collection to museums in all 50 states.How Mitchell Rales' $116 million gift will send art across AmericaThe significance of Rales' gift lies in what it will make possible beyond the National Gallery's own walls. Through Across the Nation, participating museums can select artworks from the National Gallery's permanent collection and display them on long-term loan at no cost to the borrowing institutions. The National Gallery also covers transportation, installation, insurance, training and regional marketing, removing many of the financial and logistical obstacles associated with borrowing major works. The programme also involves collaborative digital, scholarly and educational initiatives developed with participating museums. According to the National Gallery of Art, its pilot programme reached nearly 900,000 visitors at 10 partner museums after loans were installed in spring 2025. The permanent endowment means that this model of collection-sharing can now continue rather than remaining a short-term anniversary project.Why the National Gallery of Art's record gift mattersThe $116 million contribution is the largest gift ever made to endow programming at the National Gallery of Art. The museum said its scale is comparable with the institution's original founding gifts, giving the contribution significance beyond the immediate funding of a single exhibition or initiative. Rales has been a member of the National Gallery's Board of Trustees for two decades and served as its president from 2019 to 2024. His support for the museum has included major initiatives as well as gifts and assistance with acquiring important works of art. The new endowment strengthens the National Gallery's role as a national institution whose collection can be experienced by people who may never have the opportunity to visit Washington, DC. The museum's director, Kaywin Feldman, said the gift would establish Across the Nation as a core part of the Gallery's work while creating a lasting model for collaboration and collection-sharing among museums across the country.Mitchell Rales' Across the Nation programme is already reaching audiencesAlthough the $116 million endowment was announced in 2026, Across the Nation had already demonstrated its potential through its pilot phase. The first loans were installed at 10 partner museums in spring 2025, and the National Gallery reported that the programme had reached nearly 900,000 visitors during its inaugural year. Visitors told participating institutions that seeing National Gallery works alongside their local collections and exhibitions enriched their museum experience and created new connections with the artworks. The programme is designed to work with regional museums rather than simply sending individual masterpieces on occasional touring exhibitions. Partner institutions choose works that can complement their own programmes and collections, while the National Gallery provides the infrastructure and expertise required to make the loans possible. Rales had also funded the pilot programme, helping establish the model that his latest gift will now support indefinitely.The $116 million gift could bring National Gallery artworks to all 50 statesThe long-term ambition is especially striking: the National Gallery of Art intends to lend works to museums in all 50 states during the first 10 years of Across the Nation. The next programme cycle is scheduled to begin in autumn 2027 and continue through 2029, with participating institutions to be announced later. New regions will be included as the programme expands, with the goal of reaching millions of Americans who might otherwise never see the National Gallery's collection in person. The museum holds more than 160,000 works spanning the ancient world to the present, giving the initiative an enormous pool of art from which partner institutions can select. Rather than asking audiences to travel to Washington to encounter the collection, the programme is designed to take selected works into communities themselves. Rales said the gift would deepen access to the nation's collection throughout the country in perpetuity, while the National Gallery described the initiative as part of its vision of being a museum “of the nation and for all the people.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Police launch investigation into swastikas graffitied during break-in at Pardes Hanna-Karkur school
articles.summary: Several swastikas were graffitied across the windows and tables of an art classroom at the school, in addition to other destruction of property caused in the...
articles.body:
Swastikas graffitied in art room and property destroyed during break-in at Pardes Hanna-Karkur school, prompting Israel Police investigation.

Pardes Hanna-Karkur Local Council condemns incident, stating that racism, hatred, and violence have no place in the education system or community.

Police collecting evidence and searching for suspects in connection with the vandalism and break-in at Shvilim school.

Several swastikas were graffitied across the windows and tables of an art classroom at the school, in addition to other destruction of property caused in the room.

Israel Police launched an investigation into the vandalism and break-in at Pardes Hanna-Karkur's Shvilim school on Sunday morning.

Police are currently collecting evidence and searching for suspects.

"We view with great severity any expression of racism, hatred and violence, and in particular the use of Nazi symbols," the Pardes Hanna-Karkur Local Council said in a Sunday statement condemning the incident. "Such acts have no place in our education system and our community."

"We will continue to work resolutely to maintain a safe, respectful and ethical educational space, and we will not tolerate manifestations of hatred, racism and violence of any kind."

articles.title: 19 lakh lives impacted as Ganga breaches flood mark in Patna
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: More than 19.57 lakh people have been affected by floods across 11 districts of Bihar as of Sunday, with authorities putting downstream are.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: More than 19.57 lakh people have been affected by floods across 11 districts of Bihar as of Sunday, with authorities putting downstream areas on high alert. This comes after the Ganga, following heavy rain, crossed its previous highest flood level at Gandhi Ghat in Patna.The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016. While the trend was stable at Gandhi Ghat, authorities warned that Hathidah and subsequent gauge stations could be affected over the next one to three days.The rising water levels have prompted heightened vigilance across several downstream districts, with officials monitoring river levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas and keeping rescue machinery ready.19.57 lakh people affected across 11 districtsAccording to officials, flooding has affected around 19.57 lakh people in 330 gram panchayats across Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur, Begusarai, Buxar, Samastipur, Munger, Katihar and Araria.The latest figures indicate a worsening impact compared with earlier assessments, when around 16.85 lakh people across 61 blocks and 300 gram panchayats had been reported affected.With several rivers continuing to flow above danger levels, authorities have intensified relief and rescue operations in the affected districts.The Water Resources Department has warned that the Ganga at Hathidah may also cross its previous HFL, increasing the risk for Begusarai, Lakhisarai, Munger, Bhagalpur and Katihar.“Officials and field-level authorities have been directed to remain alert and continuously monitor water levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas, while taking precautionary measures as required.“Engineers have been asked to keep flood-control resources and machinery ready. People in affected areas have been advised to avoid going near the river and remain cautious,” the advisory stated.Local administrations have also been asked to keep a close watch on boat operations, prevent overloading and ensure residents receive regular updates about the flood situation.Ganga breaches danger levels at several locationsThe Ganga is above the danger mark at several locations in Bihar.At Buxar, the river was 0.08 metres above the danger mark, although its level was declining. At Dighaghat in Patna, it was 1.54 metres above the danger mark, while at Gandhi Ghat it stood 1.96 metres above it.At Hathidah, the Ganga was 1.74 metres above the danger mark and continued to rise. Munger recorded a level 0.51 metres above the danger mark, with the river showing a rising trend.The river was also 2.01 metres above the danger mark at Sultanganj and 0.65 metres above it at Bhagalpur. The Ganga remained above the danger mark at Kahalgaon as well.At Pandarak in Patna, the river was flowing at 43.92 metres at 6 am, 0.19 metres above its previous HFL of 43.73 metres recorded on August 16, 2021.In contrast, the Ganga remained below the warning level in Prayagraj and Varanasi. Its level was rising in Prayagraj but declining in Varanasi.Several rivers remain above danger levelsThe flood threat is not confined to the Ganga. Several other rivers in Bihar are also flowing above their respective danger levels.The Gandak is above the danger mark at Dumariaghat and Hajipur, while the Kosi has crossed the mark at Baltara and Kursela. The Budhi Gandak is above the danger level at Khagaria.The Punpun is above the danger mark at Sripalpur, while the Bagmati has crossed it at Benibad. The Ghaghra is also flowing above the danger level at Darauli.The combination of rising river levels and further rainfall has kept authorities on alert, particularly in downstream and low-lying areas.Relief operations expanded across flood-hit districtsThe administration has deployed significant resources to assist people affected by the floods.A total of 110 community kitchens are currently operating in various districts to provide food to affected residents. Earlier official figures had put the number of operational community kitchens at 80, with around 1.21 lakh people receiving meals through them.One relief camp is also operational, providing accommodation, food, medical assistance and other essential facilities to 326 flood-affected people.Authorities have distributed around 45,900 polythene sheets and 11,700 dry ration packets as part of relief efforts.Boats are being used extensively to evacuate residents and maintain movement in areas affected by rising waters. The latest deployment stands at 1,345 boats across the state, compared with 1,158 reported earlier.SDRF, NDRF teams deployedWith the possibility of further flooding, 27 State Disaster Response Force teams and 10 National Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed across different districts.The teams have been tasked with undertaking rapid relief and rescue operations, while district administrations continue to monitor vulnerable areas and river embankments.Officials have also been instructed to ensure that flood-control equipment and machinery remain ready for deployment as required.Rain forecast raises concern over further riseThe flood situation could remain challenging over the coming days as the Bihar Meteorological Service Centre has forecast light to moderate rainfall at several places across the state over the next two days.Heavy rainfall is also possible at some locations.Authorities are therefore preparing for the possibility of further increases in river levels, particularly in areas already affected by flooding. The state government and district administrations are continuing to monitor the situation and deploy relief materials, boats and rescue teams according to local requirements.Rail services affected on Patna-Gaya sectionThe flooding has also disrupted railway operations in parts of the state.The East Central Railway said on Sunday that some trains had been cancelled or diverted because of the “alarmingly high water level at bridge number 21" connecting Punpun and Parsa Bazar stations on the Patna-Gaya section.The development adds to the disruption caused by rising waters as authorities continue to focus on evacuation, relief and the safety of residents in flood-affected areas.Barrage discharge levelsBarrage discharge data recorded at 9 am on Sunday showed that the Sone Barrage at Indrapuri was releasing 2,27,739 cusecs of water, although the flow was declining.The Kosi Barrage at Birpur was releasing 1,68,400 cusecs, with the discharge remaining stable. The Gandak Barrage at Valmikinagar was releasing 1,29,000 cusecs, also with a stable trend.With multiple rivers remaining above danger levels, further rainfall forecast over the next two days and the Ganga already having crossed its previous HFL at Gandhi Ghat, authorities have urged residents in vulnerable areas to remain cautious and avoid approaching swollen rivers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
articles.summary: The remains of thousands more people are believed to be buried under destroyed and damaged buildings in Gaza.
articles.body:
Palestinians in northern Gaza hold funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from destroyed buildings in Zeitoun neighbourhood.

Civil defence crews and family members have been digging through rubble for weeks to recover the remains, many of which are bone fragments and belongings found on the bodies.

Gaza's civil defence service is facing challenges in recovering an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble due to a shortage of heavy machinery and equipment, with the process potentially taking years if proper resources are not provided.

Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City's Zeitoun neighbourhood.

The remains were carried on Sunday by family members from Zeitoun to al-Ma'madani cemetery in central Gaza City for burial, according to Al Jazeera's correspondent at the scene, Ghazi al-Aloul.

Civil defence crews and family members had spent weeks digging through the ruins of homes hit during Israel's genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Many of the victims were part of the extended Malaka family, which alone lost 55 members.

Al-Aloul said families had waited a long time to be able to bury their loved ones in "known, proper cemeteries". He said that the chance to bury the remains of family members was "not available to every family", noting that Israeli forces had destroyed and dug up cemeteries elsewhere in Gaza during the war.

Al-Aloul said the remains, though wrapped in shrouds resembling intact bodies, were often only fragments.

"These are bone remains and remnants of belongings that may have been found on the bodies, especially the children's," he said, adding that no complete bodies had been recovered from the site because "the Israeli occupation has prolonged this process, and continues to prolong it and prevent it from being completed quickly".

Raed al-Dahshan, head of Gaza's civil defence service, told Al Jazeera his teams had formulated plans to carry out recovery operations for thousands more missing bodies, but said the work was being held back by a shortage of heavy machinery.

"We don't have equipment, we don't have protective equipment" for rescue workers, he told Al Jazeera.

Dahshan said the recovery of an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble could be completed in about 90 days with proper equipment, but "if that equipment is barred from entering Gaza … this work will continue for years".

He said his agency had submitted a detailed list of needed equipment to international institutions and was willing to have that machinery remain under international control rather than with the civil defence directly.

He said crews needed large excavators, personal protective equipment and search equipment to locate remains urgently.

On identifying remains, he said crews rely on survivors and neighbouring families to establish who was in a building and where they were at the time of the strike, supported by a team of engineers who sort and document findings in the field. He said Israeli forces' failure to warn residents before strikes meant "dozens, even hundreds" of homes still required excavation.

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territories, told Al Jazeera that the scenes were a reminder of "the brutality of this conflict", noting some of the remains dated back to November 2023.

"Thousands of people are still languishing under this rubble … We're talking about areas that may be under Israeli military control, 70 percent of Gaza – there's difficulty accessing these areas to extract these bodies."

"Accountability must happen … It's essential that we preserve the evidence we've been able to obtain during this sensitive period."

Gaza's Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 wounded since October 2023.

Similar recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies of people from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families who were killed in a single strike, as well as more than 500 bodies from the Al-Taj tower site, officials and activists said.

articles.title: From 105mm firepower to battlefield networking: What makes China’s Type 100 tank different
articles.summary: International News: China’s next-generation Type 100 main battle tank has appeared in new footage from an unidentified Chinese city, offering a fresh look at the vehicle .
articles.body: China’s next-generation Type 100 main battle tank has appeared in new footage from an unidentified Chinese city, offering a fresh look at the vehicle in a previously unseen camouflage scheme and potentially signalling that its deployment is moving beyond parade and training appearances.Military Watch Magazine reported the footage on September 5, amid unconfirmed reports that the Type 100 is being introduced in larger numbers.China’s Ministry of National Defense has confirmed that the tank has been commissioned into the People’s Liberation Army after making its public debut at the September 2025 Victory Day parade.The Type 100 represents a significant shift in China’s approach to armoured warfare, combining conventional tank firepower and protection with an unmanned turret, active protection, advanced sensors, hybrid-electric propulsion and networked battlefield capabilities.Tank designed for the modern battlefieldChina officially describes the Type 100 as a new-generation main battle tank. Chinese state media has highlighted its unmanned turret, advanced radar, active protection system and augmented-reality technology.The vehicle appears to be armed with a 105mm main gun, while cameras and sensors positioned around the hull provide its crew with greater visibility and threat detection.Its active protection system is built around a four-faced phased-array radar designed to detect incoming projectiles, rockets and missiles and cue interceptors against them. The system is intended to provide another layer of protection against threats that increasingly include drones and precision-guided weapons.The Type 100 also incorporates hybrid-electric propulsion. According to a US Army assessment, the system can generate substantial onboard electrical power for sensors and defensive systems while allowing the tank to operate in partial or full-electric modes. This could reduce its acoustic and infrared signatures in certain operating conditions.Unmanned turret changes crew layoutOne of the Type 100’s most notable features is its unmanned turret.Unlike conventional tanks where crew members occupy the turret, the Type 100 places its three-person crew inside the hull. The commander, gunner and driver are therefore separated from the turret and its ammunition systems.The configuration can potentially improve crew protection while allowing the vehicle to use a more compact turret design.The approach reflects a broader evolution in tank design as militaries seek to protect crews from increasingly lethal anti-armour weapons, loitering munitions and drone attacks.More than a conventional tankThe Type 100 is also designed to function as part of a wider digital combat network rather than as an isolated armoured vehicle.The US Army War College has assessed the platform as being intended for long-range rapid deployment, tactical deep assault, urban operations and joint fire guidance.Its sensors and communications systems can allow the tank to receive and share battlefield information with other elements of a combat formation.The concept potentially enables the Type 100 to draw on information from drones, satellites and command headquarters to build a broader picture of the battlefield and share targeting information with other units.This means the tank could engage or support targets beyond the immediate line of sight of its crew, depending on the availability and reliability of the wider network.The result is a tank designed not simply to move, shoot and survive, but to operate as a networked battlefield node, linking sensors, weapons and commanders across a wider combat formation.A tank built around survivabilityThe Type 100’s combination of active protection, advanced sensing, hybrid propulsion and crew separation reflects the changing nature of armoured warfare.Modern tanks face threats from traditional anti-tank missiles as well as drones, loitering munitions, precision artillery and increasingly sophisticated battlefield surveillance.China’s new platform appears designed around the premise that surviving this environment requires more than thicker armour. It requires detecting threats earlier, reducing the vehicle’s signature, intercepting incoming weapons and sharing battlefield information faster.The Type 100 therefore represents a broader evolution in China’s armoured vehicle development, bringing together firepower, protection, mobility and networked warfare in a single platform.
